title: The History of Ramen — The Noodle America Accidentally Created
fullText: Over 120 billion servings. That is how many instant ramen noodles the world consumed last year alone. Not over a decade, not across a century. In a single year, enough ramen was eaten to give roughly 15 servings to every man, woman, [music] and child on the planet. And the country most people credit for this, Japan, did not actually invent the dish. The noodle came from China. The wheat came from America. And the man who made it instant was born in [music] Taiwan. Ramen, the food that defines Japanese cuisine on every continent, is really the product of three countries that never sat down and planned any of it. So, how did a bowl of soup that started in the back alleys of a port city become the most consumed, manufactured food in human history? That story is stranger than anything you would guess. The year was 1868 and Japan had just cracked open its doors to the outside world for the first time in over two centuries. The Maji restoration ended the Tokugawa Shogunates policy of near total isolation and suddenly foreign merchants, diplomats, and workers were arriving on Japanese shores. Among the earliest and most numerous were Chinese traders and laborers [music] who settled in the port city of Yokohama, just south of Tokyo. By the early 1880s, a thriving Chinatown had taken root there, complete with restaurants serving dishes that most Japanese people had never tasted before. Similar Chinese communities were growing in the port cities of Coobe and Nagasaki, too. Each one bringing its own regional cooking traditions from mainland China. One of the most [music] popular items on those Yokohama restaurant menus was a Chinese noodle soup. The noodles themselves were [music] made from wheat flour mixed with a baking soda solution called Cansui, which gave them a distinctive yellow color, a springy chew, and a slightly alkaline [music] smell that was completely unlike anything in the Japanese noodle tradition of sober and udon. In Cantonese, this style of handpulled noodle was called lame man, meaning stretched out noodles. Japanese customers [music] loved the dish, but struggled with the Chinese pronunciation, and over time, lamian [music] became ramen. Though the name came from the Chinese word for pulled noodles, the ramen that developed in Japan did [music] not actually descend from the northern Chinese Lamian tradition. Instead, it evolved from southern Chinese noodle dishes [music] from Guangdong province, reflecting the backgrounds of the immigrants who had settled in Yokohama. But here is the thing. The earliest versions of ramen [music] in Japan were not called ramen at all. Japanese diners referred to them as Sheena sober [music] or Nankin sober, names that directly reference China and the city of Nanjing. The dish was understood as [music] foreign food. A cheap and filling import eaten mostly by laborers [music] and students who could not afford fancier Japanese cuisine. It was not part of the national [music] identity. It was not celebrated. It was just a warm bowl of noodles from across the sea, eaten quickly [music] and without much ceremony at doside eeries and street stores. That started to change around the turn of the century. In 1884, a restaurant in the northern port city of Hakodate called [music] Yawwakan began serving a salt-based noodle soup that closely resembled modern shio ramen. It was among the earliest known examples of Japanese restaurants adapting the Chinese original [music] to local preferences. But the real turning point came in 1910 when a restaurant called Ry Ryiken opened in the Asakusa neighborhood of Tokyo. Ryiken was Japan's first dedicated ramen shop, and it was a sensation. The owner hired Chinese cooks from Yokohama's Chinatown to prepare the noodles, but the broth was adapted to suit Japanese tastes, lighter [music] and cleaner than the heavier Chinese originals. On its busiest days, Ryiken was selling 3,000 bowls. Lines stretched down the block in Asakusa, which was already one of Tokyo's liveliest entertainment districts. For the first time, ramen was not just a foreign curiosity. It was becoming a Japanese obsession. And within a few decades, mobile ramen carts called [music] yatai started appearing on street corners across Tokyo, Osaka, and beyond. Each one developing its own regional spin on the broth, the toppings, and the noodle thickness. These rolling noodle kitchens became a fixture of the urban night. Their charcoal [music] smoke and savory steam drawing in factory workers and late night drinkers [music] alike. But ramen was still a niche food, popular in cities, but hardly a national staple. It took a world war to change that. And the role America played in ramen's explosion is one of the strangest chapters in food history. When Japan surrendered in August of 1945, [music] the country was devastated. American firebombing campaigns had leveled entire cities. Tokyo, Osaka, Kobe, [music] Nagoya, all reduced to rubble and ash. The agricultural system had collapsed. Rice patties had been abandoned or destroyed during the fighting. And millions of Japanese citizens, soldiers returning home from the front lines, and civilians who had survived the bombings were starving. Malnutrition [music] was rampant across the country. People were collapsing in the streets of Osaka and dying of hunger in broad daylight. The situation was dire enough that food riots were a real concern and the occupying American forces knew it. The United States, which now controlled [music] Japan under General Douglas MacArthur's occupation authority, had a serious geopolitical problem. Washington was watching the spread [music] of communism across Asia with growing alarm. China had fallen to Mao [music] Dong's communist forces. Korea was teetering on the brink of a civil war that would soon [music] split the peninsula in two. American strategists believed, and they were probably right, that hungry populations were vulnerable [music] to communist recruitment. If Japan's people could not eat, they might look east to the Soviet Union and communist [music] China for answers. And the last thing the United States wanted in 1946 was a communist Japan sitting in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. So America did something that would quietly reshape Japanese food culture for the rest of the century. The US government began flooding Japan with surplus American wheat. Shiploads of grain arrived at [music] Japanese ports and the wheat was distributed through official occupation channels, school lunch programs, and civilian relief networks. Japanese school children started eating bread for [music] lunch instead of rice as part of a national school lunch program subsidized by American [music] Grain. It was an almost unthinkable cultural shift. For centuries, rice had been the center of every [music] Japanese meal, woven into religious rituals, seasonal celebrations, [music] and daily life at every level of society. And now, a generation of children was growing up eating wheat for lunch every single day. The school lunch program was so [music] effective at changing dietary habits that the United States continued providing free wheat for it even after the formal occupation [music] ended in 1952. The Japanese people had a name for this imported flower. They called it [music] Americen co, a phonetic adaptation of the English word American because everyone knew exactly where this wheat was coming from. American wheat flour, cheap, abundant, available. And here is where the ramen connection [music] catches fire. Japanese soldiers returning from deployments in China during the war had developed a taste for Chinese-style noodle soups. They came home craving wheat noodles and pork broth. At the same time, their country was swimming in cheap American wheat, but desperately short of rice. The combination was almost too perfect. Street vendors and black market stall operators, many of them demobilized soldiers with no other work, began cooking wheat noodles in makeshift broth and selling them from push carts at railway stations. Ramen stalls popped up in bombedout neighborhoods and around factory gates where [music] workers streamed in for the grueling shifts that would drive Japan's postwar reconstruction. These stalls operated in the gray zone between legal and illegal using ingredients from the massive black markets that had sprung up across occupied Japan. The historian George Salt, [music] who wrote the definitive account of Ramen's political history using declassified US government documents, traced the connection clearly. The abundance of American wheat combined with returning war veterans who carried knowledge of Chinese cuisine created the conditions for ramen to explode in popularity. The United States was not trying to create a noodle empire. Washington was trying to prevent a communist revolution, but the side effect of that cold war [music] food strategy was that ramen went from a niche city street food to a daily staple for millions of Japanese workers [music] in less than a decade. Think about that for a second. The wheat that made ramen cheap enough for every factory worker in Osaka and every dock worker in Yokohama to eat twice a day came from farms in Kansas, Nebraska, [music] and the Great Plains. American agricultural policy designed in Washington conference rooms to fight the Cold War accidentally turned a Chinese immigrant dish into the backbone of the Japanese workingclass diet. Nobody in the State Department planned it. Nobody at [music] the Pentagon predicted it. It just happened because hungry people will always find the fastest path to a hot meal. By the late 1950s, ramen was firmly established as a working person's food across Japan, but it was still something you had to go out [music] and buy from a stall or a small shop. There was no way to eat ramen at home unless you made the noodles and broth from scratch, which most people simply did not have the time or the skill to do. That gap between demand and convenience is where the most unlikely inventor in food history enters the picture. Momuku Ando was born on March 5th, 1910 in what is now Chi, Taiwan, when the island was under Japanese colonial rule. Both of his [music] parents died when he was young and he was raised by his grandparents who ran a textile shop in the city of Tynan. By his early 20s, Ando had started his own clothing business selling knitted goods and moved to Osaka, Japan, where he founded a trading company. He was an entrepreneur by instinct, always chasing the next venture. Always looking for a problem [music] to solve. But the war destroyed him. American firebombing leveled his company, his warehouse, and nearly everything he owned. He rebuilt after the war, started new businesses and lost everything again through bankruptcy. Then he was arrested for tax related issues connected to a charity he was running and spent time [music] in prison. By the time he walked free, Ando was in his late 40s with almost nothing left to show for decades of work. And then one freezing night in Osaka, he saw the line. Walking near Osaka station, Ando passed through a black market area and noticed [music] a long queue of people shivering in the cold, waiting for a bowl of ramen from a makeshift street stall. The line stretched on and on. Workers, [music] families, old men hunched against the wind. All of them waiting patiently for the same thing, a hot, cheap, filling bowl [music] of noodles. Ando stood there watching and later recalled telling himself something that would define the rest of his life. Peace will come when people have food. He decided right [music] there to find a way to make ramen that anyone could prepare at home quickly and cheaply with nothing but boiling water. What followed was an entire year of obsessive experimentation in a small wooden shed he had built behind his house in the city of Iicada in Osaka Prefecture. [music] Ando worked alone with common kitchen tools, a crude noodle machine, a cooking pot, and a stove. He had no laboratory, no research team, no corporate funding, and nobody advising him. Just a man in his late 40s in a backyard shed with flour, water, oil, [music] and an idea that everyone around him probably thought was ridiculous. He woke before dawn every morning and worked late into the night running [music] experiment after experiment. The problem he had set for himself was deceptively difficult. He needed noodles that could be dried completely and stored on a shelf for months without spoiling, without losing their flavor, and without turning to mush or staying crunchy when you [music] finally added hot water. The rehydration had to be fast, 2 or 3 minutes [music] at most, or the whole concept of instant noodles would fall apart. He tried salting the noodles to draw out moisture. He tried sunrying them for days. He tried pressing and compressing them into dense sheets. Nothing worked the way he needed [music] it to. The noodles either crumbled, refused to absorb water properly, or came back with a texture that was nothing [music] like real ramen. The breakthrough came from his own kitchen. One day, Ando was watching his wife prepare tempura, the classic Japanese deep fried batter. He noticed that the hot oil drew moisture out of the flour coating rapidly, leaving it crispy and completely dry. That observation [music] clicked something into place. What if he could do the same thing to noodles? He began flash frying cooked noodles in hot oil, which [music] dehydrated them almost instantly while creating thousands of tiny pores in their structure. When you added boiling water later, the water [music] rushed back into those pores and rehydrated the noodle in about 2 minutes. It was the exact same principle as tempura applied to [music] ramen. Simple, elegant, and nobody had ever tried it before. On August 25th, 1958, Ando launched his creation to the public. He called it chicken ramen, choosing chicken flavor because [music] he believed chicken was eaten in virtually every culture on Earth and would give the [music] product the widest possible appeal. The noodles came in a single dried block with the seasoning already [music] baked in. You just added hot water, waited 2 minutes, and you had a steaming bowl of ramen. [music] The price was 35 yen per serving. For comparison, a fresh bowl from a street vendor cost around 6 yen. So, chicken ramen was actually [music] expensive, nearly six times the price of the real thing. It was considered a luxury item at first, but it sold anyway because the convenience factor was unlike anything that had ever existed in the Japanese [music] food market. People called it magic ramen. Nobody had ever seen food work like this. You pour water on a dry block and 2 minutes later you [music] are eating noodle soup. It seemed impossible. Ando renamed his company Nissen Food Products and began scaling up production. Within a year, [music] Mitsubishi Corporation stepped in to help promote and distribute chicken ramen nationwide. Sales accelerated rapidly. By the early 1960s, instant ramen had become a fixture in Japanese [music] homes, especially among workers with short lunch breaks and students cooking in tiny one- room apartments. Yet, Ando was not finished. The man who had already changed how Japan ate was about to change how the entire planet ate. And once again, the inspiration came from America. In 1966, Ando traveled to the United States on a fact-finding tour to explore whether chicken ramen could crack into Western markets. During a meeting with buyers at an American supermarket chain, something happened that completely reshaped his thinking. The American managers wanted to [music] try his product, but they had no Japanese Donbury Bowls in their office. They did not own chopsticks. So, they improvised. They broke the [music] dried noodle block in half, dropped the pieces into paper coffee cups, poured in hot water, [music] and ate the noodles with forks. Ando stood there watching Americans eat his invention in a way he had never imagined. And a realization hit him. His [music] product assumed that the person eating it already owned a bowl. In Japan, that was a safe assumption. In the rest of the world, it was not. If he wanted ramen to go truly global, the container had to come with the noodle. He spent the next 5 years [music] developing what would become cup noodles. The engineering was far more complex than most [music] people realize. Ando discovered that suspending the noodle block inside the cup rather than resting it flat on the bottom made the entire package more durable and less [music] likely to crack during shipping. The polystyrene cup itself served three [music] functions at once as packaging material, cooking vessel, and eating bowl. Each [music] unit came with a small foldable plastic fork tucked inside. The design was deceptively simple. You peeled back the foil lid, [music] added hot water, waited 3 minutes, and ate directly from the cup. You did not need a bowl. You did not need a kitchen, and there was nothing to clean up afterward. Cup Noodles launched on September 18th, 1971. And initially, it struggled. The product cost about four times more than a standard packet of instant ramen, and Japanese supermarkets were hesitant to stock something so unfamiliar. [music] Walking around while eating was considered rude in Japanese culture, and cup noodles seemed designed for exactly that. Sales were slow in the opening months. Then, 5 months later, something completely unrelated to noodles changed everything. In February of 1972, five armed members of the United Red Army, a [music] radical far-left militant group, took a woman hostage inside a mountain lodge called Assama Sanso near the resort town of Karuizawa in Nagano Prefecture. What followed [music] was a 10-day siege that became the first marathon live television broadcast in Japanese history. The rescue operation on the final day ran 10 hours and 40 minutes of continuous [music] coverage. Nearly 90% of the country tuned in to watch the standoff unfold in real time. Camera crews captured riot police assembled in the freezing mountain snow, armored trucks inching up narrow paths, and sharp shooters positioned on the ridge lines surrounding the barricaded lodge. But viewers noticed something else during those long winter hours of footage. Outside the lodge, police officers waiting in the snow between shifts were eating something from small [music] cups. Something steaming, something you could hold with one gloved hand. The cameras caught it again and again. Officers slurping cup noodles in the cold, getting a fast hot meal without leaving their positions. Nobody at Nissen had planned this. There was no product placement deal, no marketing arrangement with the police. Officers had simply grabbed whatever was convenient from nearby stores. [music] But the effect on the viewing public was enormous. Tens of millions of Japanese households saw cup noodles being used in a real crisis. Providing hot food in freezing mountain conditions with zero preparation beyond [music] adding water. The following week, sales skyrocketed. Cup noodles became a household name overnight, driven by the most improbable advertising anyone could imagine. a hostage crisis. No marketing agency on Earth could have planned what happened [music] at that mountain lodge in Nagono. And Ando, the man who had watched people line up in the cold for noodles [music] 25 years earlier, now watched a different kind of line form. Customers at convenience stores and supermarkets across Japan, grabbing cup noodles off shelves as fast as Nissen could stock them. By the end of the 1970s, instant ramen had conquered Japan completely, and Nissen was expanding aggressively into Asia, Europe, and the Americas. But something surprising was happening with fresh ramen back in Japan. The instant version had not [music] killed the ramen shop. If anything, it had done the opposite. By turning ramen into a daily [music] habit for tens of millions of people, instant noodles had created a massive audience that also craved the crafted real broth version. Regional ramen styles that had been quietly developing for [music] decades suddenly found a national and then international audience hungry for them. In Saporro on the northern island of Hokkaido, chefs had been perfecting miso [music] based ramen with rich, heavy broth and thick curly noodles since the 1950s. Down in Hakarta on the southern island of Kyushu, tonkotu [music] ramen made by boiling pork bones for hours until the broth turned opaque. White had become a regional obsession. That milky tonkatsu broth was reportedly created by accident in Fukuoka in 1947 when restaurant cooks overboiled their pork stock and decided to serve it anyway rather than dump it. Customers ended up preferring the deeper, richer flavor. Tokyo contributed its own tradition of Shooyu ramen built on soy sauce-based broth and lighter shio ramen seasoned with salt. Each city, each neighborhood, each individual ramen master developed a proprietary [music] blend of broth, noodle texture, and toppings that became a point of fierce local pride. Ramen shops became the kind of places where regulars argued over which bowl was best, where chefs guarded their recipes with almost paranoid secrecy, and where a line out the door meant you had found something worth waiting for. In 1994, the obsession reached a new level. The Shin Yokohama Ramen Museum opened [music] as the world's first food themed amusement park. Its basement levels recreated [music] a 1950s Tokyo streetscape in painstaking detail, complete with vintage storefronts, old movie posters, [music] and period appropriate street vendors. Inside those recreated shops, visitors could taste ramen from famous regional shops across Japan without ever boarding a train. [music] The museum proved something the food industry had not fully grasped. Ramen was not just a quick meal anymore. [music] It was a cultural experience, a craft tradition, a form of regional [music] identity that people would travel across the country to explore and debate and rank. Then came the moment that would have been unthinkable to anyone who remembered ramen's origins as cheap immigrant street food sold from push carts. In 2015, a tiny 9-seat restaurant in Tokyo called Japanese Sober Noodles, Tsuta, became the first ramen shop in the world to receive a Michelin star. The founder, Onishiuki, had created a signature soy sauce ramen featuring Italian black truffles that married European [music] fine dining ingredients with Japanese noodle craftsmanship. A bowl of noodles that had started in the back alleys of Yokohama [music] Chinatown that had fueled starving workers buying from black market stalls that had been freezedried in a backyard [music] shed by a bankrupt inventor was now sitting in the same Michelin guide as legendary restaurants in Paris and New York. Today, the global instant noodle market alone is valued at over $ 36 billion. More than 120 billion servings are consumed every year across the world. China leads with roughly 44 billion servings annually. Indonesia eats nearly 15 billion and the United States, the country whose wheat accidentally fueled ramen's rise in the first place, now consumes over 5 billion servings per year. Fresh ramen shops have spread [music] across every continent from Brooklyn to Berlin to Bangkok to Buenosire with chefs in each city adapting the dish to local ingredients and local tastes. In New York, shops serve ramen with smoked [music] brisket. In London, you can find ramen topped with English cheddar. In [music] Sao Paulo, Japanese Brazilian fusion bowls feature ingredients that would confuse a traditionalist in Tokyo. And that adaptation is not corruption. It is exactly what happened when Chinese Lamian first crossed the sea to Yokohama 140 years ago. The cycle keeps repeating itself [music] because ramen has always been a dish that absorbs whatever culture it lands in. Momuku Ando lived to see all of it. He spent his final years pursuing a lifelong dream of making ramen available literally everywhere, including outer space. In 2005, Japanese astronaut Nguchi [music] Soichi ate a speciallydesed version called Space Ram aboard the International Space Station. Ando died in 2007 at the age of 96. Still thinking about new ways to feed people. The man who had lost everything in the war, who had gone bankrupt and been jailed, who had stood watching hungry people wait [music] in the cold for noodles, had created a food consumed by billions of people in more than 100 countries. And the strangest part of the whole story is that none of it was supposed to happen this way. Chinese immigrants carried the noodle to Japan. American cold war strategy provided the wheat. A Taiwanese-born inventor in a Japanese shed figured out how to dry it. American supermarket managers showed him how to put it in a cup. A televised hostage crisis made it famous. Every single turning point was an accident, a coincidence, or a side effect of something else entirely. Ramen is not the product of one country [music] or one culture. It is what happens when three countries crash into each other at exactly the right moments across 140 years of history. And you are tasting the result every time you peel [music] back that lid and pour in the hot water. If you enjoyed this one, hit subscribe and leave a comment telling us your favorite style of ramen. fullTextVi: Hơn 120 tỷ phần ăn. Đó là số lượng mì ramen ăn liền được thế giới tiêu thụ riêng trong năm ngoái. Không phải hơn một thập kỷ, không phải qua một thế kỷ. Chỉ trong một năm, số lượng mì ramen đã được ăn đủ để cung cấp khoảng 15 phần ăn cho mọi đàn ông, phụ nữ, [âm nhạc] và trẻ em trên hành tinh. Và đất nước được nhiều người tin tưởng nhất vào điều này, Nhật Bản, đã không thực sự phát minh ra dish. Món mì đến từ Trung Quốc. Lúa mì đến từ Mỹ. Và người đàn ông đã làm được điều đó ngay lập tức sinh ra ở [âm nhạc] Đài Loan. Ramen, món ăn định hình nền ẩm thực Nhật Bản ở mọi châu lục, thực sự là sản phẩm của ba quốc gia chưa bao giờ ngồi xuống và lên kế hoạch cho bất kỳ điều gì trong số đó. Vậy bát canh bắt đầu từ con hẻm phía sau một thành phố cảng trở thành nơi sản xuất và tiêu thụ thực phẩm nhiều nhất trong lịch sử loài người? Câu chuyện đó kỳ lạ hơn bất cứ điều gì bạn có thể đoán. Năm đó là năm 1868 và Nhật Bản vừa mới mở cửa cho thế giới bên ngoài lần đầu tiên sau hơn hai thế kỷ. Việc khôi phục Maji đã chấm dứt chính sách gần như cô lập hoàn toàn của Mạc phủ Tokugawa và đột nhiên các thương gia, nhà ngoại giao và công nhân nước ngoài đã đến bờ biển Nhật Bản. Trong số những người sớm nhất và nhiều nhất là thương nhân và người lao động [âm nhạc] Trung Quốc đã định cư ở thành phố cảng Yokohama, ngay phía nam Tokyo. Vào đầu những năm 1880, một khu phố Tàu thịnh vượng đã bén rễ ở đó, với đầy đủ các nhà hàng phục vụ những món ăn mà hầu hết người Nhật chưa từng nếm thử trước đây. Các cộng đồng người Hoa tương tự cũng đang phát triển ở các thành phố cảng Coobe và Nagasaki. Mỗi người đều mang truyền thống nấu ăn của vùng từ Trung Quốc đại lục. Một trong những món [âm nhạc] phổ biến nhất trong thực đơn nhà hàng Yokohama đó là Súp mì Trung Quốc. Bản thân sợi mì là [âm nhạc] được làm từ bột mì trộn với baking soda giải pháp có tên Cansui, mang lại cho chúng màu vàng đặc biệt, nhai có độ đàn hồi và một mùi [âm nhạc] hơi kiềm, hoàn toàn không giống bất cứ thứ gì trong mì Nhật truyền thống tỉnh táo và udon. Trong tiếng Quảng Đông, kiểu mì kéo tay này được gọi là người què, nghĩa là kéo dài ra mì. Khách hàng Nhật Bản [âm nhạc] yêu thích món ăn nhưng gặp khó khăn với cách phát âm tiếng Trung và hơn thế nữa thời gian, lamian [âm nhạc] đã trở thành ramen. Mặc dù cái tên này xuất phát từ từ tiếng Trung có nghĩa là mì kéo, nhưng món ramen được phát triển ở Nhật Bản [âm nhạc] không thực sự bắt nguồn từ truyền thống Lamian phía bắc Trung Quốc. Thay vào đó, nó phát triển từ món mì [âm nhạc] miền Nam Trung Quốc từ tỉnh Quảng Đông, phản ánh nguồn gốc của những người nhập cư đã định cư ở Yokohama. Nhưng đây là điều. Những phiên bản đầu tiên của ramen [âm nhạc] ở Nhật Bản hoàn toàn không được gọi là ramen. Thực khách Nhật Bản gọi chúng là Sheena tỉnh táo [âm nhạc] hoặc Nankin tỉnh táo, những cái tên đó trực tiếp tham khảo Trung Quốc và thành phố Nam Kinh. Món ăn được hiểu là [âm nhạc] món ăn nước ngoài. Một mặt hàng nhập khẩu rẻ và đầy đủ được người lao động [âm nhạc] và sinh viên có thể sử dụng chủ yếu không đủ khả năng ẩm thực Nhật Bản sang trọng hơn. Nó không phải là một phần của bản sắc [âm nhạc] dân tộc. Nó đã không được tổ chức. Chỉ là tô mì nóng hổi từ bên kia biển vào, ăn cho chóng vánh [âm nhạc] và không có nhiều nghi lễ tại các quán rượu và cửa hàng ven đường. Điều đó bắt đầu thay đổi vào khoảng đầu thế kỷ.
